line: Hallo. This is Liam, in for Bear. A language model knows what it read in training. But it can also look things up. Today: what changes when the model searches the web — and what it costs you.
screen: Hook card reading 'what the model knows vs what it can look up'. A book glyph (training) and a globe with a magnifier glyph (search) slide together into one mark.

line: Four terms before we start. Grounding: letting the model search the web before it answers. Freshness: how new the facts are. Cost per query: what each search is billed at. Blocked page: a site the search can't get into. Keep those four in your pocket.
screen: Four term cards appear one by one: 'Grounding — search the web before answering' / 'Freshness — how new the facts are' / 'Cost per query — what each search is billed at' / 'Blocked page — a site the search can't get into'.

line: The test was one question, asked twice. He needed control arms for a Dodge Grand Caravan, and he needed to buy them in Canada. Same question, two modes. First: no grounding. Just the model, its memory, nothing else.
screen: The question card: three chips appear one by one — 'control arms' / 'Dodge Grand Caravan' / 'Canada' — then a 'times two' badge lands: asked twice.

line: The ungrounded answer was fine. Generic. It knew what control arms are. It could talk about the part. But no current prices. No Canadian stores. No idea what shipping looks like this week. An answer from memory — and memory has a cutoff date.
screen: The question card plus a grey answer card: three greyed rows appear one by one — 'generic part info' / 'no current prices' / 'no stores' — each with a grey dot; a tag reads 'from memory only'.

line: Then the same question, with grounding on. The model searched first, then answered. Now there were retailers. Real stores, in Canada. Shipping times. Prices as they are right now, not as they were when the model trained. Same question — a completely different answer.
screen: Search arrows fly from the question card to a fresh answer card; three rows appear one by one with green checks: 'current prices' / 'Canadian retailers' / 'shipping times'; a 'fresh' tag lands on the card.

line: Read the two side by side and the difference is obvious. Ungrounded: a good explanation of the part, no facts you can act on. Grounded: fewer words about the part, more words about the buying. One tells you what it is. The other tells you how to get it.
screen: Two columns side by side: 'ungrounded' (grey card) versus 'grounded' (white card with green checks); rows land in pairs with cross and check marks; a divider arrow between the columns.

line: Three things grounding added. Current prices — not guesses, today's numbers. Canadian retailers — places you can actually order from, not stores that won't ship to you. And shipping reality: what's in stock, how long it takes. That's the whole value of grounding: facts you can act on.
screen: Three cards appear one by one, each with a dot and a green check: 'current prices' / 'Canadian retailers' / 'shipping reality' — the three things grounding added.

line: But grounding has a limit, and it's worth seeing. Some product pages block the search crawler — no access, no data. The model can't read what it can't reach. So the grounded answer can still have holes. Grounding is a window, not a skeleton key.
screen: A globe with a brick wall across it; three page cards appear one by one, each stamped 'blocked' with a red cross; a greyed-out block reads 'holes remain'.

line: Now the price. Grounding isn't billed by the token. It's billed by the search — per one thousand queries. Each grounded question costs you a search on top of the tokens. Cheap for one question. Real money if you ground everything, every time.
screen: A meter card: coins stack one by one onto a coin slot; the label reads 'billed per 1k queries'; a token counter sits greyed out and crossed off.

line: So when do you ground? Here's the film's rule of thumb. If the answer changes with time — prices, stock, this week's news — ground it. If the question is timeless — how a part works, how to write the code — save the search. Grounding is a tool, not a default.
screen: A toggle switch; two paths branch: 'timeless question' (toggle off, tag 'memory') versus 'fresh facts needed' (toggle on, tag 'ground it'); a pointer lands on each path in turn.

line: Let's recap. Act one: the same question twice — memory gives you an explanation, grounding gives you facts. Act two: grounding adds prices, retailers, and shipping — but it can't reach blocked pages. Act three: grounding is billed per search, so use it when freshness matters.
screen: A recap card; three lines appear one by one: 'memory explains, grounding informs' / 'adds facts, can't beat blocked pages' / 'billed per search — use it when fresh'.

line: Your turn. Think of one question the model can't answer from training — something that happened this week, or a price right now. Ask it ungrounded. Then ask it grounded. Compare the two, and notice what changed.
screen: A your-turn card: 'Pick one fresh question. Ask it ungrounded. Ask it grounded.' Below: 'Notice what changed.'

line: Muse, in for Bear. Thanks for watching. Next film: Structured Outputs — we make the model fill in a form. Grounded Answers. At Nik Bear Brown.
